teaching.causalExplanation: They count the way we count anything in bulk, with a counting unit. A dozen always means twelve, and a ream of paper is always five hundred sheets. Twelve eggs or twelve watermelons, it's still a dozen. If you buy five dozen, you know you've got sixty, without counting each one. Chemists use a counting unit too, and it's called the mole. One mole is six point zero two two times ten to the twenty-three particles. That number is called the Avogadro constant, after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro. It's written N A, and its unit is per mole, because it tells you how many particles are in each mole. When we count a substance in moles, that's its chemical amount. Its symbol is a small n, and its unit is the mole, written m o l. How big is that number? If you counted one particle every second, without stopping, one mole would take about nineteen million billion years. That's more than a million times the age of the universe. Yet a mole of water molecules is only about a tablespoon. That's how small particles are.
